mainTopic: שבת 103b: The minimum act of writing that makes one liable, how many חטאות one brings, and closed versus open letters
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא that reads the verse "וְעָשָׂה מֵאַחַת" to find the smallest act of writing that makes one liable on שבת. The ת"ק says you are liable for writing a short name that is part of a longer name, like שם from שמעון. רבי יהודה says even two identical letters, like שש, are enough. רבי יוסי says the real source is רושם, marking the beams of the משכן, so even scratches count. רבי שמעון says one is liable only for a מלאכה of a lasting kind. The גמרא then explains that the identical-letters view is really רבן גמליאל's. It also works out that רבי שמעון, who is usually lenient, requires a whole word but not a whole verse. Next, רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא explains how רבי יוסי reads "one" and "these" in the verse, which teaches when a person brings one חטאת for many acts and when he brings one for each act. Finally, רב חסדא learns from שם inside שמעון that a closed letter written open is valid. A ברייתא challenges him, and the גמרא defends him with רבי יהודה בן בתירה's מים hint for ניסוך המים. The גמרא then begins to question that proof, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The word 'one' limits liability
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings the word "אחת" in the verse to show that a tiny fragment, such as a single letter, is not enough for liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: "one" (a whole unit).
steps.whatsHappening: On the previous amud, the ברייתא suggested that because of the word "מאחת" (from one), even one letter might make you liable. Now it answers that the verse also says "אחת", which means a complete unit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse has two words that seem to clash. "מאחת" suggests that part of an act is enough. "אחת" suggests that a whole act is needed. This line brings in the second word, so that the ברייתא can now reconcile the two.

keyTerms.meaning: "The verse teaches": a phrase that introduces a source from the פסוק
From one: part of a unit

steps.confusionAlert: This amud starts in the middle of a ברייתא. The word "מאחת" was already discussed right before this point. Here we only see the second half of the derivation.

phrases.english: The verse states: "one."
phrases.notes: Pushes back against the idea that a single letter is enough.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided derivation that began on the previous amud.
steps.raayaObject: That a single letter is not enough for liability.

steps.title: A small name taken from a larger name
steps.stepSummary: The ת"ק reconciles the two words: you are liable for writing a short name that is also the beginning of a longer name.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? You are not liable until you write a small name that comes from a big name: "שם" from שמעון and from שמואל, "נח" from נחור, "דן" from דניאל, "גד" from גדיאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks how both words can be true at once. It answers with a case that is both "part" and "whole."
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose a person meant to write שמעון but only wrote "שם". That is part of the bigger name, which fits "מאחת". But "שם" is also a full name on its own, which fits "אחת". So one case satisfies both words of the verse.

keyTerms.meaning: "How so?": a formula for reconciling two sources that seem to conflict
A small name taken from a bigger name

steps.whatToRemember: According to the ת"ק, the minimum for כותב is two letters that already form a real, complete word, even if the person planned to write more.

phrases.english: How so?
He is not liable until he writes
a small name out of a big name:
"Shem" from Shimon or from Shmuel,
"Noach" from Nachor, "Dan" from Daniel,
"Gad" from Gaddiel.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא כֵּיצַד, אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיִּכְתּוֹב שֵׁם קָטָן מִשֵּׁם גָּדוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the tension between "מאחת" and "אחת".
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Writing a short complete name that is part of a longer name makes one liable.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: two identical letters are enough
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rules that writing two letters of the same kind, which together form a word, makes one liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: even if he wrote only two letters and they are one name (the same letter twice), he is liable. For example: שש, תת, רר, גג, חח.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה adds a broader opinion that makes one liable more easily: you are liable even for two letters that are the same letter repeated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ת"ק's examples all use two different letters. רבי יהודה teaches that a word made of one letter written twice also counts. Even though it is the same letter repeated, it still forms a meaningful unit.

keyTerms.meaning: One name: here, the same letter repeated

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ לֹא כָּתַב אֶלָּא שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת
phrases.english: Even if he wrote only two letters
and they are one kind of letter, he is liable,
for example: shesh, tet, rar, gag, chach.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֲפִילּוּ לֹא כָּתַב אֶלָּא שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a case of liability beyond the ת"ק's examples.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two identical letters forming a word make one liable.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: the liability is really for marking
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי challenges the whole premise: the liability is not for כותב but for רושם, as was done on the beams of the משכן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי said: Is he really liable because of writing? He is only liable because of marking, since they would mark the beams of the משכן to know which beam was the partner of which.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי questions the basis of the earlier opinions. He says the real source of liability is making marks, not writing letters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every מלאכה on שבת comes from work done in the משכן. רבי יוסי points out that the משכן had no "writing". It had signs marked on beams so that matching beams could be set up together. So what matters is making a meaningful mark, not forming a written word.

keyTerms.meaning: "Is it really so?": a rhetorical challenge
Writing: one of the ל"ט מלאכות

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a basic method: we define a מלאכה by checking what was actually done in the משכן.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei said:
Is he really liable because of writing?!

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲלֹא אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם רוֹשֵׁם,
phrases.english: Isn't he liable only because of marking,
since they would mark the beams of the Mishkan
to know which one is its partner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: וְכִי מִשּׁוּם כּוֹתֵב הוּא חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the basis that both the ת"ק and רבי יהודה assume.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that liability here comes from writing letters.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source in the משכן was marking beams, not writing, so the definition must follow marking.

steps.title: Scratches are enough for liability
steps.stepSummary: Because the source is marking, a single scratch across two boards, or two scratches on one board, makes one liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore: if he made one scratch across two boards, or two scratches on one board, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי draws the practical result of his view: even marks that are not letters at all make one liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A single scratch running across two boards shows that those boards belong together. That is exactly what the משכן markings did. Two scratches on one board also form a sign. No letters are needed.

phrases.aramaic: לְפִיכָךְ, שָׂרַט שְׂרִיטָה אַחַת עַל שְׁנֵי נְסָרִין,
phrases.english: Therefore, if he made one scratch across two boards,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שְׁתֵּי שְׂרִיטוֹת עַל נֶסֶר אֶחָד — חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: or two scratches on one board, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְפִיכָךְ, שָׂרַט שְׂרִיטָה אַחַת עַל שְׁנֵי נְסָרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבי יוסי's principle of רושם.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meaningful scratches, even without letters, make one liable.

steps.title: רבי שמעון: the word 'from one' shows a whole is not required
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון begins his own derivation. One might think you must finish the whole name, garment, or sieve, so the verse says "מאחת".
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: "And he did one". I might think he is not liable until he writes the whole name, weaves the whole garment, or makes the whole sieve. So the verse says "from one".
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון starts a new reading of the same verse. He first uses "מאחת" to show that you do not need to finish the entire project.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taken alone, "אחת" could mean the complete project, such as the whole name or the whole garment. The word "מאחת" teaches that part of the project is enough. רבי שמעון expands the discussion beyond writing to weaving and sieve-making.

keyTerms.meaning: "I might have thought": introduces a possible but wrong reading

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says: "And he did one";

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל עַד שֶׁיִּכְתּוֹב אֶת כָּל הַשֵּׁם,
phrases.english: I might think: only once he writes the whole name,
only once he weaves the whole garment,
only once he makes the whole sieve;
the verse says: "from one."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: ״וְעָשָׂה אַחַת״, יָכוֹל עַד שֶׁיִּכְתּוֹב אֶת כָּל הַשֵּׁם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens רבי שמעון's separate derivation from the same verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Finishing the entire project is not required.

steps.title: But a single letter or thread is too little
steps.stepSummary: If "מאחת" means even a tiny part, then one letter or one thread would be enough. So the verse also says "אחת".
steps.simpleTranslation: If "from one", I might think he is liable even if he wrote only one letter, wove only one thread, or made only one hole of the sieve. So the verse says "one".
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון now sets a limit in the other direction, so that "מאחת" is not stretched too far.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "מאחת" taken alone could include the smallest possible act. "אחת" blocks that reading. Now both extremes are excluded: finishing the whole project is not needed, and a tiny bit is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: one hole or cell of the sieve

phrases.english: If "from one,"

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל אֲפִילּוּ לֹא כָּתַב אֶלָּא אוֹת אַחַת,
phrases.english: I might think: even if he wrote only one letter,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲפִילּוּ לֹא אָרַג אֶלָּא חוּט אֶחָד,
phrases.english: even if he wove only one thread,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲפִילּוּ לֹא עָשָׂה אֶלָּא בַּיִת אֶחָד בַּנָּפָה —
phrases.english: even if he made only one hole in the sieve;
the verse says: "one."

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי ״מֵאַחַת״, יָכוֹל אֲפִילּוּ לֹא כָּתַב אֶלָּא אוֹת אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the expansion from the previous step.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects stretching "מאחת" to a single letter, thread, or hole.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Such a tiny act is not a complete unit, which is what "אחת" requires.

steps.title: רבי שמעון: liability requires a lasting kind of work
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון reconciles the two words: you are liable only for a מלאכה whose kind lasts.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? He is not liable until he does a מלאכה whose kind lasts.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון gives his rule for reconciling "אחת" and "מאחת".
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ת"ק measured the minimum by "a small name inside a big name." רבי שמעון measures it instead by permanence. The act must be the type of work that endures, even if the whole project is not finished.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון's rule is that liability on שבת requires a מלאכה of a lasting kind. This is a different measure from the ת"ק's "small name inside a big name."

phrases.english: How so?
He is not liable until he does a labor
whose kind endures.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא כֵּיצַד? אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה מְלָאכָה שֶׁכַּיּוֹצֵא בָּהּ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the tension between steps 6 and 7.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Liability requires a מלאכה of a lasting type.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: sometimes one offering, sometimes many
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי reads the verse as "he did one" and "he did these": sometimes one חטאת covers many acts, and sometimes each act needs its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: "And he did one" and "and he did these". Sometimes he is liable one offering for all of them, and sometimes he is liable for each and every one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי uses the same verse for a completely different topic: how many חטאות one must bring for several violations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The odd wording "מאחת מהנה" hints at both "one" and "these." From this, רבי יוסי learns that there are cases where many sins are counted as one for the קרבן, and cases where each is counted separately. The גמרא will later explain exactly which cases these are.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not about the minimum amount for writing. רבי יוסי moves to a different question: how many קרבנות are owed.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
"And he did one", "and he did these":
sometimes he is liable one for all of them,

phrases.aramaic: וּפְעָמִים שֶׁחַיָּיב עַל כׇּל אַחַת וְאַחַת.
phrases.english: and sometimes he is liable for each and every one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different use of the same verse, about counting קרבנות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The verse teaches that there are cases of one חטאת for many acts and cases of a חטאת for each act.

steps.title: רבי יהודה seems to contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא quotes רבי יהודה as saying that even two identical letters make one liable. This clashes with his view elsewhere that two different letters are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, the ברייתא teaches: רבי יהודה says that even if he only wrote two letters of the same kind, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a ברייתא and points out a quote from רבי יהודה that seems to contradict what he says elsewhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Elsewhere, רבי יהודה requires two different letters, like the 'שם' inside 'שמעון'. Here he says two of the same letter, like 'שש', is enough. Those two positions cannot both be his.

keyTerms.meaning: In any event, it teaches (pointing to a key line in a source)
One type (two of the same letter)

phrases.english: In any event, it teaches:
Rabbi Yehuda says

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ לֹא כָּתַב אֶלָּא שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת
phrases.english: even if he wrote only two letters
and they are the same letter, he is liable.
phrases.notes: 'שם אחד' here means one kind of letter repeated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the derivations of רבי שמעון and רבי יוסי back to רבי יהודה's view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The consistency of רבי יהודה's position
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One source has him requiring different letters, while this ברייתא has him accepting identical letters.

steps.title: One view is his own, the other is his teacher's
steps.stepSummary: There is no real contradiction. One statement is רבי יהודה's own opinion, and the other is his teacher's opinion, which he reports.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is his own view, and that one is his teacher's view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction by saying the two statements come from two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה himself requires two different letters. The broader line, which makes one liable even for identical letters, is really רבן גמליאל's view, which רבי יהודה was only passing on.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is his own view, that is his teacher's view.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דִּידֵיהּ, הָא דְרַבֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the sources between two speakers
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both statements are רבי יהודה's own opinion.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the view requiring two different letters is his own. The view that makes one liable even for two identical letters belongs to his teacher, רבן גמליאל.

steps.title: Proof that the lenient view is רבן גמליאל's
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows רבי יהודה quoting רבן גמליאל: two identical letters, such as שש or גג, make one liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: רבי יהודה says in the name of רבן גמליאל: even if he only wrote two identical letters, he is liable. Examples are שש, תת, רר, גג, חח.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to back up its answer. It shows that the lenient view really comes from רבן גמליאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'משום רבן גמליאל' show that רבי יהודה was reporting his teacher's ruling. Each example is a real word made of one letter written twice.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל:
phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabban Gamliel:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ לֹא כָּתַב אֶלָּא שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת
phrases.english: even if he wrote only two letters
and they are the same letter, he is liable,
such as 'shesh', 'tet', 'rar', 'gag', 'chach'.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: That the identical-letters view belongs to רבן גמליאל
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where רבי יהודה quotes רבן גמליאל
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה himself requires two different letters. רבן גמליאל holds that two identical letters are enough.

steps.title: Isn't רבי שמעון saying the same as the תנא קמא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי שמעון's rule differs from the תנא קמא's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't רבי שמעון's view the same as the תנא קמא's?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to רבי שמעון and asks what he adds that the first opinion did not already say.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא requires a small word that makes sense. רבי שמעון requires a מלאכה of a kind that lasts. In practice these sound like the same rule, so why is it a separate opinion?

keyTerms.meaning: The first (unnamed) opinion in the ברייתא

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon is the same as the first Tanna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about רבי שמעון's view from step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: Whether רבי שמעון's opinion has its own content
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A named Tanna who says nothing new seems pointless.

steps.title: A suggested difference: two א's used in amulets
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a difference: writing two א's (as in אאזרך). The תנא קמא says not liable. רבי שמעון says liable, because amulets regularly use that combination.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say the difference between them is two א's, as in 'אאזרך'. The תנא קמא holds that for two א's he is not liable. רבי שמעון holds that since this combination appears in ordinary amulets, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible answer, which it will test right away. It suggests the two opinions differ over letters that are not a real word but are commonly written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two א's are not a word, so the תנא קמא would not make one liable. But amulets use this pair, so for רבי שמעון it counts as lasting, meaningful writing. That would make רבי שמעון stricter.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (a suggestion about to be tested)
There is a difference between them

steps.confusionAlert: 'וכי תימא' is not the גמרא's final answer. It is a suggestion that the very next line will reject.

phrases.english: And if you say
that alef alef of 'a'azercha' is the difference between them,
that the first Tanna holds
that for alef alef of 'a'azercha' he is not liable,
and Rabbi Shimon holds
since it appears in ordinary amulets, he is liable,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא אָלֶ״ף אָלֶ״ף דַּ״אֲאַזֶּרְךָ״ אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes an answer to step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing to a practical case where the two views differ
steps.terutzMaskana: They would differ on two alefs, with רבי שמעון stricter. (This is rejected next.)

steps.title: Would רבי שמעון really be the stricter one?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא doubts that רבי שמעון would be stricter than the תנא קמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that רבי שמעון is the stricter one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion. It is setting up a proof that רבי שמעון tends to be lenient in these cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggested difference only works if רבי שמעון is stricter. The גמרא finds that unlikely, and it will now bring a source to show it.

phrases.english: Is that to say that Rabbi Shimon is to the stringent side?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the suggestion of step 14.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It makes רבי שמעון stricter, which goes against how he rules elsewhere.

steps.title: רבי שמעון is lenient: you must finish the whole job
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that drilling, scraping, tanning, or drawing even a little makes one liable. רבי שמעון says one is liable only after finishing the whole job, so he is the lenient one.
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it taught: one who drills any amount is liable. So is one who scrapes any amount, one who tans any amount, and one who draws any amount of a design on a vessel. רבי שמעון says: only once he drills the whole thing, scrapes the whole thing, tans the whole thing, or draws the whole thing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that רבי שמעון is usually more lenient. That knocks out the suggestion from step 14.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion makes one liable for any small amount. רבי שמעון requires finishing what was planned. So רבי שמעון is the lenient one, and he would not be stricter about two א's.

keyTerms.meaning: Draws a design on a vessel

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught:
one who drills any amount is liable,
one who scrapes any amount,
one who tans any amount,
one who draws a design on a vessel, any amount.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: עַד שֶׁיִּקְדַּח אֶת כּוּלּוֹ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says: not until he drills all of it,
until he scrapes all of it,
until he tans all of it,
until he draws all of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the source behind the rejection in step 15.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי שמעון is lenient, not strict, in measuring a מלאכה
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about drilling, scraping, tanning, and drawing

steps.title: New answer: רבי שמעון requires a whole word
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now says רבי שמעון's point is that one is liable only after writing the entire word.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what רבי שמעון comes to teach us: not until he writes the whole word.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer to 'how is רבי שמעון different?' He is the lenient one and requires a complete word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits his pattern of 'finish the whole thing'. The תנא קמא accepts a small part of a bigger word, like שם out of שמעון. רבי שמעון requires the whole word that was planned.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הָא אֲתָא לְאַשְׁמוֹעִינַן,
phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Shimon comes to teach us this:
not until he writes the entire word.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הָא אֲתָא לְאַשְׁמוֹעִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 14 with one that matches step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new practical difference between the opinions
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי שמעון is stricter about two א's.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי שמעון is lenient and requires the whole word.

steps.title: But רבי שמעון himself said a whole word is not needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: רבי שמעון's own teaching from the verse says 'one might think you need the whole word, so the verse says מאחת'. That means a whole word is not required.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you say this? Wasn't it taught that רבי שמעון says: 'and he did one' might mean not until he writes the whole word, so the verse says 'from one'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new answer by quoting רבי שמעון's own teaching (from step 6), which seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 6, רבי שמעון used 'מאחת' to reject the idea that you must write the whole word. So he cannot also be the one who requires the whole word.

phrases.english: And can you say this?
But wasn't it taught, Rabbi Shimon says: 'and he did one',

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל עַד שֶׁיִּכְתּוֹב אֶת הַשֵּׁם כּוּלּוֹ —
phrases.english: one might think not until he writes the entire word,
so the verse says 'from one'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי שמעון requires a whole word
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His own ברייתא uses 'מאחת' to say that a whole word is not necessary.

steps.title: Fixing the wording: 'whole verse', not 'whole word'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the wording of רבי שמעון's ברייתא. 'מאחת' teaches that you don't need the whole verse, but you still need a whole word.
steps.simpleTranslation: Fix it and say it this way: one might think he is not liable until he writes the whole verse, so the verse says 'from one'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the clash by changing one word in the ברייתא: 'the whole word' becomes 'the whole verse'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now 'מאחת' only removes the need for a full verse. Writing one complete word is enough. That leaves רבי שמעון free to require a whole word, so the answer of step 17 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Fix the text and say it this way

steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון: you are liable only after writing a whole word. You do not need to write a whole verse. The תנא קמא accepts even a smaller word inside a bigger one.
steps.confusionAlert: This changes how we read רבי שמעון's teaching in step 6. Its 'the whole word' is now read as 'the whole verse'.

phrases.english: Fix it and say this:

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל עַד שֶׁיִּכְתּוֹב אֶת הַפָּסוּק כּוּלּוֹ —
phrases.english: one might think not until he writes the entire verse,
so the verse says 'from one'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18 by correcting the text.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'מאחת' teaches that a whole word is not needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'מאחת' teaches that a whole verse is not needed. A whole word is still required.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the rule for רבי שמעון: the smallest amount of writing that makes one liable is one complete word.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: sometimes one offering, sometimes many
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי reads the פסוק as 'he did one' and 'he did these'. So sometimes a person brings one חטאת for all his violations, and sometimes he brings one for each.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: 'And he did one' and 'and he did these.' Sometimes a person owes one offering for all of them, and sometimes he owes an offering for each one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now returns to quote רבי יוסי's line from the ברייתא, already seen in step 9, so that it can explain it. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The odd wording 'מאחת מהנה' is read as two phrases: 'one' and 'these.' 'One' points to cases where all the sins join together into one חטאת. 'These' points to cases where each sin counts separately. רבי יוסי does not yet say which case is which. That comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And he did from one of these' (ויקרא ד:ב), the פסוק about bringing a חטאת
Liable to bring one offering for all of them
For each and every one separately

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
'And he did one,' 'and he did these':
phrases.notes: The verse 'מאחת מהנה' is read as if it said both phrases.

phrases.english: sometimes he is liable one offering for all of them,

phrases.aramaic: וּפְעָמִים שֶׁחַיָּיב עַל כׇּל אַחַת וְאַחַת.
phrases.english: and sometimes he is liable for each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: וְעָשָׂה אַחַת וְעָשָׂה הֵנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The analysis of רבי שמעון is finished. The גמרא now moves on to analyze רבי יוסי's statement from the ברייתא, first quoted in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק teaches two outcomes: sometimes one חטאת covers many violations, and sometimes each violation needs its own חטאת.

steps.title: What is רבי יוסי's source?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא asks how רבי יוסי gets his rule from the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי son of רבי חנינא said: What is רבי יוסי's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא asks how רבי יוסי reads all of this out of the words. This question sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי only gave a conclusion: 'sometimes one, sometimes many.' The question asks which words in the פסוק produce that conclusion. The same speaker will answer it.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason or source?
An אמורא, not the same person as the תנא רבי יוסי

steps.confusionAlert: There are two people here. רבי יוסי is the תנא in the ברייתא. רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא is a later אמורא who explains him.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina said:
What is the reason of Rabbi Yosei?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind רבי יוסי's statement in step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which words in the פסוק teach that sometimes there is one חטאת and sometimes many.

steps.title: Four readings from 'one,' 'from one,' 'these,' 'from these'
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק could have said 'אחת' and 'הנה'. Instead it said 'מאחת' and 'מהנה'. So we get four lessons: 'one,' 'part of one,' 'these,' 'part of these.' We also get two mixed cases: 'one that is these' and 'these that are one.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'One' and 'from one'; 'these' and 'from these'; a 'one' that is really 'these,' and a 'these' that is really 'one.'
steps.whatsHappening: The answer: every word and every extra letter מ in the פסוק carries its own lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra מ turns each word into two readings: the full thing, and a part of the thing. The words 'one' and 'these' are also mixed together into two crossover cases. In the first, a single thing splits into many. In the second, many things merge into one. This is only the list of headings. The next step explains each one.

keyTerms.meaning: 'From one,' meaning part of one thing
'One' that is really 'these': a single thing that counts as many
'These' that are really 'one': many things that count as one

phrases.english: 'One' and 'from one,'
'these' and 'from these,'
'one' that is 'these,'
and 'these' that is 'one.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 21 by listing the readings of the פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra מ in 'מאחת' and 'מהנה' gives extra readings, and mixing 'one' with 'these' gives the two crossover cases.

steps.title: Explaining each of the four readings
steps.stepSummary: 'One' is writing שמעון, and 'from one' is writing שם out of שמעון. 'These' are the אבות מלאכות, and 'from these' are the תולדות. 'One that is these' is knowing it is שבת but not knowing the מלאכות are forbidden: one חטאת for each מלאכה. 'These that are one' is forgetting it is שבת but knowing the מלאכות are forbidden: one חטאת for everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'One' means writing 'שמעון.' 'From one' means writing 'שם' out of 'שמעון.' 'These' means the main categories of labor (אבות). 'From these' means the sub-categories (תולדות). 'One that is these' means he knew it was שבת but did not know the labors were forbidden. 'These that are one' means he forgot it was שבת but knew the labors were forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives a real example for each of the four readings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'From one' means you are liable even for a part, like writing שם, which is part of שמעון. 'From these' adds the תולדות to the אבות. In זדון שבת ושגגת מלאכות, his mistake is about each מלאכה separately, so each one needs its own חטאת. Here 'one,' שבת, becomes 'these.' In שגגת שבת וזדון מלאכות, his only mistake is that it is שבת, a single mistake, so he brings one חטאת. Here 'these' become 'one.'

keyTerms.meaning: The main categories of forbidden labor on שבת
Sub-categories, labors that come from the main ones
Not knowing that these labors are forbidden
Knowing that these labors are forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. When he knows it is שבת, he brings many offerings, one for each מלאכה he did not know about. When he forgot it is שבת, he brings only one offering. The rule: count the separate mistakes.
steps.whatToRemember: How many חטאות a person brings depends on how many separate mistakes he made. If he forgot it was שבת, that is one mistake and one חטאת. If he did not know the מלאכות were forbidden, each מלאכה is its own mistake and its own חטאת.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic rule for counting חטאות on שבת. It is discussed at length earlier in מסכת שבת, in פרק כלל גדול.

phrases.english: 'One': writing 'Shimon,'
'From one': writing 'Shem' out of 'Shimon.'
'These': the main labors; 'from these': the sub-categories.
'One' that is 'these':
he knew it was Shabbat but did not know the labors were forbidden.
phrases.notes: He brings a separate offering for each labor.

phrases.english: 'These' that is 'one':
he forgot it was Shabbat but knew the labors were forbidden.
phrases.notes: He brings one offering for all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fills in the four headings from step 22 with real cases.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each reading has a case: partial writing, תולדות, many חטאות when he knows it is שבת, and one חטאת when he forgot it is שבת.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: a small name inside a big name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to רבי יהודה's line in the משנה. We find a small name, like שם, inside a bigger name, like שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said: We find a small name taken from a big name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה to look at רבי יהודה's words. This sets up a question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה supports liability for partial writing. A short name can be found inside a longer one, like שם inside שמעון, so writing it counts as writing. The גמרא is about to test whether the example really fits.

keyTerms.meaning: A short name taken out of a longer name

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said:
We found a small name from a big name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves away from the ברייתא and back to a quote from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing a small name that is part of a larger name, like שם from שמעון, counts as real writing.

steps.title: But the מ״ם is different in each word
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the example really fits. In שם the מ״ם is the final, closed ם. In שמעון it is the open מ. So the letters are not the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it really the same? The מ in 'שם' is closed (ם), and the מ in 'שמעון' is open!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה's example. Writing שם as part of שמעון uses a different letter shape than the word שם itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone set out to write שמעון and stopped after 'שמ', his מ is open (מ). But the real word שם ends with a closed ם. So it seems he has not really written the word שם, and the proof should not work.

phrases.english: Is it similar?
The mem of 'Shem' is closed,
the mem of 'Shimon' is open!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the example given in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's example of שם from שמעון
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The letters are not the same shape (open מ versus closed ם), so 'שמ' taken from שמעון is not really the word שם.

steps.title: רב חסדא: a closed letter written open is still valid
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא learns from here that writing a closed letter in open form is still valid. So the open מ still counts as writing שם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: This teaches that if a letter should be closed and someone wrote it open, it is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא accepts רבי יהודה's example and draws a new rule from it: the open or closed shape of the מ does not ruin the writing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא does not reject the question's facts. He turns the משנה into a source: since the משנה treats שמ with an open מ as the word שם, a closed letter written open must be valid. That answers the question, and it also teaches a rule about valid writing.

keyTerms.meaning: This teaches us (a rule we learn from the source)
And he made it (wrote it that way)

steps.whatToRemember: An open מ written where a closed ם belongs still counts as valid writing. That is why writing שם out of שמעון makes a person liable.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule matters beyond שבת, for the laws of writing a ספר תורה (סתום ופתוח).

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
This is to say:
a closed letter that one made open is valid.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֹאת אוֹמֶרֶת סָתוּם וַעֲשָׂאוֹ פָּתוּחַ כָּשֵׁר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the difference in letter shape and learns from the משנה that it does not matter.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An open מ cannot stand in for a closed ם, so 'שמ' from שמעון is not the word שם.
steps.terutzMaskana: A closed letter written open is valid, so 'שמ' with an open מ counts as writing שם.

steps.title: A ברייתא demands perfect writing, with no swapping of letters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא on ״וּכְתַבְתָּם״. It forbids writing one letter in the shape of another, including closed letters as open ones. This seems to contradict רב חסדא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: 'And you shall write them' means the writing must be perfect. One may not write an א like an ע, or an ע like an א. The same goes for ב and כ, ג and צ, ד and ר, ה and ח, ו and י, ז and נ, ט and פ. One may not write bent letters as straight ones, or straight as bent. One may not write ם as ס, or ס as ם. One may not write closed letters as open, or open as closed. An open פרשה may not be made closed, and a closed one may not be made open. If one wrote it in the layout of a song, or wrote the song like regular text, or wrote without ink, or wrote God's names in gold, these must be put away (נגנז).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב חסדא with a ברייתא. The ברייתא says a closed letter may not be written as an open one, and that such a text must be put away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא said an open מ still counts as a closed ם. The ברייתא lists 'סתומין פתוחין' among the forbidden swaps, so a closed letter written open is not acceptable. The ending 'הרי אלו יגנזו' shows the text is actually invalid, not just written less nicely.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They challenged': the גמרא brings a תנאי source against a statement
Bent (middle) letters versus straight (final) letters, like כ/ך and נ/ן
Closed letters (final ם) versus open letters (regular מ)
They must be put away. The text is unusable but holy, so it is stored rather than thrown out.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two kinds of 'open' and 'closed' in this ברייתא. 'סתומין פתוחין' is about letters (ם versus מ). 'פרשה פתוחה וסתומה' is about the spacing of paragraphs. Only the letter rule challenges רב חסדא.

phrases.english: They raised an objection: 'And you shall write them'
means that it should be perfect writing
phrases.notes: A wordplay: וכתבתם read as כתיבה תמה

phrases.english: so one should not write alefs as ayins,
or ayins as alefs.
Beits as kafs, kafs as beits.
Gimmels as tzadis, tzadis as gimmels.
Dalets as reishes, reishes as dalets.
Hehs as chets, chets as hehs.
Vavs as yods, yods as vavs.
Zayins as nuns, nuns as zayins.
Tets as pehs, pehs as tets.
Bent letters as straight ones, straight ones as bent.
phrases.notes: Middle forms versus final forms, like כ/ך and נ/ן

phrases.english: Final mems as samekhs, samekhs as final mems.
phrases.notes: A closed ם looks like a ס

phrases.english: Closed letters as open ones, open ones as closed.
phrases.notes: This is the phrase that challenges רב חסדא

phrases.english: An open paragraph, one may not make it closed,
and a closed one, one may not make it open.
If one wrote it like a song,
phrases.notes: Using the special brick-like layout of שירת הים

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב אֶת הַשִּׁירָה כַּיּוֹצֵא בָהּ,
phrases.english: or wrote the song like the rest of the text,
or wrote without ink,
or wrote the names of God in gold —
these must be put away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It attacks רב חסדא's rule from step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's rule that a closed letter written open is valid
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא explicitly forbids writing 'סתומין פתוחין' and says such a text must be put away. So a closed letter written open is invalid.

steps.title: רב חסדא follows רבי יהודה בן בתירה, who finds מים in extra letters
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב חסדא agrees with a different תנא. רבי יהודה בן בתירה builds the word מים from three extra letters in the סוכות פסוקים, as a hint to ניסוך המים.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said it like this other תנא, as it was taught: רבי יהודה בן בתירה says, 'On the second day it says ונסכיהם. On the sixth day it says ונסכיה. On the seventh day it says כמשפטם. That gives מ, י, מ, which spells מים. From here there is a hint in the תורה to ניסוך המים.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב חסדא. It says he holds like a different תנא, רבי יהודה בן בתירה, who reads extra letters in the סוכות קרבנות to spell מים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three extra letters. The ם from ונסכיהם is a closed final letter. The י comes from ונסכיה, and the final ם comes from כמשפטם. When they combine into מים, the first ם must act as an open מ at the start of the word. So this תנא treats a closed letter as if it were an open one, which disagrees with the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: 'He said it like this תנא': the challenged אמורא follows a different תנאי opinion
A תנא who learns a hint from extra letters
The water libation poured on the מזבח on סוכות
A hint in the text, not a full explicit source

steps.whyThisMatters: The answer does not dismiss the ברייתא. It shows that תנאים disagree on this point. This is also the well-known תורה source hinting to ניסוך המים.

phrases.english: He (רב חסדא) said it like this תנא,

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָה אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: as it was taught: רבי יהודה בן בתירה says:
On the second day it says 'and their libations'.
phrases.notes: An extra closed ם, compared with the usual ונסכה

phrases.english: On the sixth it says 'and its libations',
on the seventh it says 'according to their law',
phrases.notes: An extra ם, compared with the usual כמשפט

phrases.english: so we have mem, yod, mem, which spells 'water',

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן רֶמֶז לְנִיסּוּךְ מַיִם מִן הַתּוֹרָה.
phrases.english: from here is a hint to the water libation from the תורה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers the challenge of step 27 by placing רב חסדא within a disagreement between תנאים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Tannaitic dispute: the אמורא follows a different תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא of כתיבה תמה seemed to be the only view, which would refute רב חסדא.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב חסדא follows רבי יהודה בן בתירה, who treats a closed ם as usable for an open מ.

steps.title: If open-made-closed is valid, closed-made-open is valid too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out the reasoning. In this דרשה, a letter is allowed to switch between open and closed form. From this, closed written as open is also valid, as רב חסדא said.
steps.simpleTranslation: And since an open letter that was made closed is valid, a closed one too, a closed letter made open, is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רבי יהודה בן בתירה's דרשה backs up רב חסדא. If one direction of switching works, the other works too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מ at the start of מים should be open, yet the תורה wrote it as the closed ם of ונסכיהם. That is a case of 'open made closed' that still counts. The גמרא treats the two directions as the same, so 'closed made open', which is רב חסדא's case, is also valid.

keyTerms.meaning: An open letter that was written in closed form

steps.whatToRemember: There is a disagreement between תנאים. The ברייתא of ״וּכְתַבְתָּם״ forbids swapping closed and open letters. רבי יהודה בן בתירה's מים hint directly shows only that an open letter written closed still counts. The step that extends this to רב חסדא's case, a closed letter written open, is questioned right away in the next step (״מִי דָּמֵי״).
steps.confusionAlert: Do not get the direction mixed up. The דרשה itself shows open made closed: the מ of מים appears as the closed ם of ונסכיהם. The גמרא then extends this to the reverse direction, which is רב חסדא's case in שמעון.

phrases.english: And since an open letter that one made closed is valid,

phrases.aramaic: סָתוּם נָמֵי סָתוּם וַעֲשָׂאוֹ פָּתוּחַ — כָּשֵׁר.
phrases.english: a closed one too, a closed letter that one made open, is valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It draws out the logic of step 28 to support רב חסדא.
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's rule that a closed letter written open is valid
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהודה בן בתירה's reading of the ם of ונסכיהם as the opening מ of מים

steps.title: Questioning whether the proof is really comparable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks, 'Is it similar?' It begins to split the case of an open letter made closed from the case of a closed letter made open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really the same? An open letter that one made closed…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof it just brought for רב חסדא from the דרשה of רבי יהודה בן בתירה. It starts to point out a difference: changing an open letter into a closed one may not be the same as changing a closed letter into an open one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 29 treated the open–closed switch in the מים דרשה as one general rule, valid in either direction. Here the גמרא suggests the two directions might have different laws. If they differ, the דרשה may not prove רב חסדא's specific case, which is a closed letter written as open. The sentence is cut off here, and the next words finish the contrast.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Is it similar?' — a formula that challenges whether two cases are truly comparable
An open letter form, like the regular מ
A closed letter form, like the final ם
'And he made it' — he wrote it in the other form

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume that open→closed and closed→open are automatically the same law. That is exactly the assumption the גמרא is now questioning. Also note that this passage stops in the middle of a sentence; the second half of the contrast comes next.

phrases.english: Is it similar?
phrases.notes: Signals that the גמרא is rejecting the comparison it just made.

phrases.english: An open letter that one made closed —
phrases.notes: The first side of the contrast. The other side (closed made open) follows on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof brought in Step 29 for רב חסדא by questioning whether the cases are truly comparable.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the support for רב חסדא from the מים דרשה, not the דרשה itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof treats open→closed and closed→open as one rule. The גמרא begins to argue that the two directions may not be equal.
